content.title: About
content.content: Butternut squash (Cucurbita moschata) is a winter squash with a bell-like shape, smooth tan skin, and sweet, nutty, deep orange flesh. It originated in the Americas and is eaten roasted, pureed, or in soups and stews. Butternut squash keeps well for months after harvest.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Butternut squash is a winter squash, harvested when fully mature and with a hard rind.
It is botanically a fruit, classed as a type of berry.
The seeds are edible and can be roasted like pumpkin seeds.
Butternut squash stores for several months in a cool, dry place.
Its flesh becomes sweeter as it cooks and as it is stored.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: The orange flesh is rich in beta-carotene, which the body can convert into vitamin A.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Provides potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals support normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Butternut squash contributes fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Butternut squash is relatively low in calories and filling.

items.title: Allergic reactions and skin irritation
items.content: Squash allergy is uncommon but can occur, and handling raw squash may irritate the skin of some people.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Butternut squash contains natural sugars and starch, so portions matter for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Potassium considerations
items.content: People with kidney problems or on certain medications should consult a healthcare professional about potassium intake.

items.title: Cutting safety
items.content: The hard rind is difficult to cut, so use a sharp knife on a stable surface or microwave the whole squash briefly to soften it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Butternut squash can be roasted in cubes or halves, steamed, boiled, mashed, pureed into soups, or added to stews, curries, risottos, pasta, and salads. It can be baked into muffins and pies. The skin is edible when roasted but is usually peeled.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole butternut squash in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place for up to a few months. Cut squash should be wrapped and refrigerated and used within about five days. Cooked squash or puree can be refrigerated for three to five days or frozen.

chicken-drumstick-grilled-with-sauce-ski.title: Chicken drumstick, grilled with sauce (skin not eaten)

content.title: About
content.content: A chicken drumstick grilled with a flavorful sauce is a tender, skin‑less piece of meat. Grilling keeps the meat juicy while the sauce adds a savory, aromatic finish. This product is common in fast‑food menus, salads, and as a standalone snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Drumsticks contain more connective tissue than breast meat, which makes them especially juicy when cooked properly.
Grilling imparts a characteristic smoky flavor that is enhanced by using charcoal or wood chips.
Tomato‑based, honey, or soy sauces are popular marinades for drumsticks, boosting taste and shelf life.
Chicken drumsticks are a staple in street food and fast‑food outlets because of their convenient size and quick cooking time.
Removing the skin reduces fat content while preserving the meat’s essential nutrients.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Drumsticks provide high‑quality protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: They are a source of vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Chicken meat supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Drumsticks contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: With the skin removed, the remaining fat is mostly monounsaturated and polyunsaturated.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people can be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: High sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain a lot of salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you have hypertension.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Drumsticks contain more cholesterol than breast meat; consume in moderation if you have cardiovascular concerns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the drumsticks hot, drizzled with any remaining sauce. They are easy to eat with hands, add to salads, rice or noodle dishes, and work well in wraps or sandwiches. Sprinkle fresh herbs or spices for extra flavor if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked drumsticks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before eating to ensure safety.

frozen-coffee-drink-decaffeinated-with-n.title: Frozen Coffee Drink, Decaffeinated, with Non‑Dairy Milk

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen coffee drink, decaffeinated, with non‑dairy milk is a refreshing beverage made from filtered coffee, caffeine removed, and a smooth plant‑based milk (soy, oat or almond). The mixture is frozen to a soft‑serve texture similar to sorbet and served in a cup or glass. It contains no dairy and is suitable for vegans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Caffeine is extracted using water or CO₂, preserving most of the coffee’s flavor notes.
Plant milks give the drink distinct flavor nuances: soy adds a mild nutty note, oat adds a sweet creaminess, almond adds a subtle aromatic finish.
Frozen coffee is popular in summer menus of cafés and restaurants, combining the bold taste of coffee with a cooling texture.
The drink can be easily adapted for dietary needs, such as adding sugar‑free sweeteners or protein powder.
In some countries frozen decaf coffee is marketed as a “healthier” alternative to ice cream because it typically contains less sugar and fat.

items.title: Low caffeine content
items.content: The absence of caffeine makes the beverage safe for caffeine‑sensitive individuals and suitable for consumption at any time of day.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee provides polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Plant milks, especially soy, add a modest amount of protein beneficial for muscle maintenance and metabolism.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Oat milk contains beta‑glucan, which promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low‑calorie dessert option
items.content: When prepared with modest sweetening, frozen decaf coffee can be a lighter alternative to traditional ice cream.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to soy, oat, or almond milk used in the drink.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Commercial versions often contain added sugar; people with diabetes should choose unsweetened or low‑sweetener options.

items.title: Cold temperature
items.content: The icy nature of the beverage can cause discomfort for those with sensitive teeth or esophageal issues.

items.title: Additive sensitivity
items.content: Stabilizers and emulsifiers are sometimes added; those with sensitivities should read the ingredient list carefully.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the frozen coffee in a cup, optionally topped with whipped plant‑based cream and a sprinkle of cinnamon or cocoa powder. Sweeten with honey, maple syrup or stevia to taste if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen coffee in an airtight container in the freezer at –18 °C. For longer storage (over 2‑3 months) sugar may crystallize, so briefly thaw in the refrigerator before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Pistachios are the edible seeds of the pistachio tree (Pistacia vera), native to Central and Western Asia. They are enclosed in a hard, beige shell that splits open naturally when the nut ripens, revealing a green kernel. Pistachios have a mildly sweet, buttery flavor and are eaten as a snack and used in desserts, baked goods, ice cream, and savory dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pistachios belong to the same plant family as cashews and mangoes.
The shell splits open naturally as the nut matures, and the opening is why pistachios are sometimes called smiling nuts.
Pistachios have been eaten for thousands of years in Central Asia and the Middle East.
Iran, the United States, and Turkey are among the major pistachio producers.
The green color of the kernel comes from chlorophyll and other plant pigments.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Pistachios provide protein, which supports muscle maintenance and fullness.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Pistachios contain mostly unsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Provides fiber
items.content: Pistachios contribute fiber, which supports normal digestion.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6, thiamin, and potassium
items.content: These nutrients support energy metabolism and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Contains lutein and zeaxanthin
items.content: These plant pigments are associated with eye health.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Pistachios can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe. People allergic to cashews may also react to pistachios.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Pistachios are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Added salt
items.content: Roasted and salted pistachios can contain a lot of sodium.

items.title: Mold and choking
items.content: Moldy nuts can contain harmful toxins and should be discarded, and whole nuts are not suitable for young children because of choking risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pistachios can be eaten as a snack straight from the shell, added to salads, yogurt, oatmeal, and baked goods, or ground into pesto, crusts, and desserts. Shelling the nuts yourself can help slow down eating. Choose unsalted or lightly salted nuts when possible.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pistachios in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, or in the refrigerator or freezer for longer storage. Keep shelled nuts away from moisture and strong odors. Discard nuts that smell rancid, taste bitter, or look moldy.
